prompt: A hiring manager has eleven candidate links open and forty minutes before a meeting. She opens yours. What is the single thing most likely to make her keep looking instead of closing the tab in the first ten seconds?

options.text: A large 'About Me' section explaining your journey into coding
A project she can actually click into and try, with a one-line description of what it does
A long list of every language and framework you've touched
A photo and a short personal bio at the very top of the page

hints: Ask what she can *do* in the first ten seconds, not what she can *read*.
A skills list is a claim. A working link is evidence. Evidence is faster to evaluate.
explanation: A clickable, working thing tells her in one action whether you can ship — no reading required. The bio, the journey, and the skills list are all claims about you; none of them can be checked in ten seconds, so a time-pressed reviewer skips straight past them looking for something she can verify herself. This doesn't mean bios or skills lists are worthless — they matter once she's already decided to look closer. It means they can't be the first thing she meets.

prompt: Statement: A portfolio homepage that lists twelve technologies you know is more convincing than one that shows three working projects.

config.statement: A portfolio homepage that lists twelve technologies you know is more convincing than one that shows three working projects.
config.rubric: Should note that a skills list is unverifiable on its own — anyone can type 'Python' — while a working project demonstrates the skill and lets the reviewer form their own opinion of your level.

hints: What can a reviewer actually check without leaving the page?
A list of nouns proves you've heard of something. A running project proves you can use it.
explanation: A list of technologies is the easiest thing on a portfolio to fake, inflate, or simply be wrong about — everyone lists more than they're comfortable being asked about in an interview. Three working projects, each doing something specific, let a reviewer form their own judgment of your actual level from evidence instead of your self-report of it.

prompt: Match each weak tech-list line to the decision-based sentence that replaces it — the kind of sentence that survives being asked 'why?'

pairs.left: Built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS
pairs.right: Used vanilla JS instead of a framework because the app is one screen with no routing — a framework would have added a build step for nothing it needed
Stores entries in localStorage rather than a database, because the app is single-user and doesn't need data to survive a browser change — the tradeoff is it won't sync across devices
Laid out with a single flex column below 600px because most users open it one-handed on a phone during a symptom flare, not at a desk

right: Chose React because it's the most popular framework right now

hints: Ask: does this sentence answer 'why did you choose this,' or just name the thing chosen?
A decision sentence names the alternative you didn't pick, and why.
explanation: The weak version names a tool. The strong version names a *choice* — what it was chosen over, and what real constraint made that the right call. 'Uses localStorage' could mean the author didn't know how to set up a database; 'localStorage because it's single-user and doesn't need to survive a browser change' proves the author considered the alternative and picked deliberately. That's the entire difference a reviewer is paying attention to.

prompt: You built a small habit tracker for people managing chronic illness — it lets someone log a symptom or a habit with one tap, no login required, data stored only in the browser. Write two sentences for the project page explaining *why* it has no login and no backend, framed as decisions rather than limitations.
hints: Name the actual constraint or user need that led to the choice, not just the choice.
It's fine for a decision to include a tradeoff you accepted — naming the tradeoff is what makes it read as a decision instead of an accident.
Avoid 'I didn't have time to add a backend' — that's true but reads as a limitation, not a decision, even when the same choice is defensible.
explanation: A strong answer names the real reason (e.g. 'no login because someone logging a symptom one-handed at 2am shouldn't have to authenticate first') and names the accepted tradeoff (data doesn't sync across devices). The weak version of this answer just restates the feature ('it has no login, data is stored locally') without ever explaining why that's good for this specific app and these specific users.

prompt: Sort each project-description phrase by what it actually is: an honest claim, an oversell, or an undersell.

items.text: Handles empty input, duplicate entries, and a slow network without crashing
A production-grade, enterprise-ready platform
Just a small thing I threw together, nothing special
Built in a weekend as a learning exercise, and it works for the one thing it's meant to do
Sorry if this isn't very good, I'm still learning
Scales to millions of users

hints: An honest claim is checkable and specific — it names a real behavior or a real scope.
An oversell uses a scale or a maturity word ('enterprise', 'production-grade', 'millions') the project has never actually been tested against.
An undersell apologizes for or minimizes something before anyone has judged it.
explanation: The honest middle category is doing something neither of the other two does: it names a specific, checkable fact — what the project handles, or what it was built for — without attaching a scale or an apology to it. Oversell claims a scale the project has never been tested at; undersell pre-emptively lowers the reader's expectations before they've even looked, which does nothing except make them trust the honest parts less too.

prompt: Rewrite this undersold sentence as an honest claim: 'It's just a basic to-do app, nothing special, I made it while learning JavaScript.' The app actually supports reordering tasks by drag-and-drop and persists state across browser refreshes.
hints: Drop 'just,' 'basic,' and 'nothing special' — none of them are facts about the app.
Lead with something the app specifically does, not with when or why you made it.
It's fine to mention it was a learning project — put that after the facts, not before them, and without apologizing for it.
explanation: A strong rewrite states the specific capabilities directly: 'A to-do app with drag-and-drop reordering and state that persists across refreshes, built while learning JavaScript.' Nothing here is exaggerated — reordering and persistence are real, checkable features — and nothing apologizes for the project before the reader has even seen it. The 'built while learning' context survives, just moved to where it belongs: after the facts, as context, not as a disclaimer.

prompt: Put these five cleanup steps in the order you'd actually do them before linking a repo on a portfolio page.

items: Remove secrets, API keys, and stray console.log statements
Rename the variables and functions that would confuse a stranger (x, data2, doStuff)
Write or update the README: what it does, how to run it, what's not finished
Add a short comment only where the code's intent genuinely isn't obvious from reading it
Read the whole thing once, start to finish, as if you were the stranger

hints: Secrets are a safety issue, not a polish issue — they come first, before anyone looks at anything else.
Names are the fastest, cheapest fix and make every step after them easier to do well.
The final read-through is a check on everything before it, so it has to come last.
explanation: Secrets first, because a leaked API key is a real cost, not a cosmetic one, and it's checked before anything else touches the repo. Names next, because confusing names make every subsequent step — writing the README, deciding what needs a comment — harder to do accurately. The README comes before comments because it's the thing most reviewers actually read; comments are for the code itself. The final read-through catches whatever the first four steps missed, which is why it has to be last, not first.

options.text: It's too short to be a real function
Nothing here — variable name, parameter name, or comment — tells a stranger what this function is for
It should use a for-loop instead of filter
It's missing a return type annotation

hints: The function runs correctly — the problem is entirely about what a reader can infer from it, not about correctness.
Try covering the function body and guessing what doStuff, d, x, and i.a mean from the names alone.
explanation: `doStuff`, `d`, `x`, and `i.a` carry zero information about what this function actually does — filtering, say, active users, or in-stock items, or valid entries. The commented-out old version adds a second question ('is this still needed?') with no answer. None of this is a bug; the code works. But 'this is a portfolio piece meant to show someone I can build things' includes 'someone can read what I built,' and right now nobody can, in under a minute, without running it.

prompt: Statement: A portfolio with thirty small projects demonstrates more skill than one with three, because it shows more range.

config.statement: A portfolio with thirty small projects demonstrates more skill than one with three, because it shows more range.
config.rubric: Should note that a reviewer can't evaluate thirty projects in the time they have, and a page of mostly-unfinished tutorial clones reads as unfinished work rather than range, while three deep, finished, explained projects are actually checkable.

hints: Think about how many of thirty projects a reviewer with ninety seconds can actually look at.
What does a portfolio of thirty tutorial-clone repos actually prove, versus what it's meant to prove?
explanation: Range is only valuable if it's checkable, and nobody scanning a portfolio in under two minutes is going to open thirty links. In practice, a long list reads as a list of tutorials followed once each — which is real learning, but isn't the same signal as 'I can take something from idea to finished, working, explained thing.' Three deep projects, each with a live link, a decisions-based description, and clean code, are actually checkable in the time available, and check for exactly the thing a reviewer is trying to determine.

prompt: You have six projects. Sort each into 'keep on the portfolio' or 'leave off' using the criteria from this lesson: finished, live/runnable, explains a specific decision, and reasonably recent.

items.text: A budget tracker, finished, live, README explains the localStorage decision, built two months ago
A todo-app tutorial clone, followed step by step, never deployed, no changes of your own
An API-backed recipe app, finished, live, explains the caching decision, built three weeks ago
A half-finished chat app abandoned after two days, not runnable
A CSS animation experiment, finished and live, but no decisions to explain — it's a visual demo, not a tool
A habit tracker, finished, live, README explains the offline-first decision, built last year

hints: A tutorial followed exactly, with no changes, doesn't demonstrate anything beyond 'I completed a tutorial.'
Unrunnable and unfinished projects cost more than they're worth — a broken link actively hurts more than an absent one.
A polished demo with nothing to explain still fails the 'explains a decision' bar, even though it's finished and live.
explanation: Three of the six survive all four criteria; the other three each fail on one specific criterion — the tutorial clone fails 'explains a decision' (there were none to make), the abandoned chat app fails 'finished' and 'runnable' outright, and the CSS demo fails 'explains a decision' even though it's genuinely finished and live. Notice that 'finished and live' alone isn't sufficient — a portfolio project has to earn its place on all four criteria, not just some of them.

prompt: Which opening line gets a reviewer to click through?

options.text: Hi, welcome to my portfolio! I'm a passionate self-taught developer.
I build small tools for tracking things — budgets, symptoms, habits.
Skills: HTML, CSS, JS, React, Node, Python, SQL, Git

hints: Which of these could a reviewer actually verify by clicking something?
explanation: The middle option is specific and points at a category of real, clickable work. The other two are, respectively, unverifiable enthusiasm and an unattached list.

prompt: Rewrite this sentence so it's an honest, checkable claim instead of an oversell: 'A production-grade e-commerce platform built for scale.' (It's actually a single-product checkout demo with three pages.)
hints: Name what it actually does — the product, the checkout flow — not a scale it's never been tested at.
explanation: A strong rewrite names the real scope honestly: 'A three-page checkout flow for a single product, built to practice cart state and a simulated payment step' — specific, checkable, and not claiming anything the project can't back up.

prompt: Rewrite this sentence so it drops the apology without becoming an oversell: 'Just a little project, not much really, a basic weather app.' (It actually handles a failed API call gracefully and shows a cached forecast.)
hints: Lead with the specific behavior — the failed-call handling — not with 'just' or 'basic'.
explanation: A strong rewrite states the specific, real behavior directly: 'A weather app that falls back to a cached forecast if the API call fails' — no apology, no inflated claim, just what it actually does.

prompt: Sort each project-page sentence.

categories: Decision (names an alternative and a reason)

items.text: Chose SQLite over a hosted database because the app is single-user and doesn't need concurrent writers
items.category: Decision (names an alternative and a reason)

items.text: Uses SQLite
Built with React
Used React instead of vanilla JS because the app has five interacting views that all needed to share state
items.category: Decision (names an alternative and a reason)

hints: A decision names what was chosen *over*. A claim just names what was chosen.
explanation: The decision-shaped sentences each name an alternative and a reason; the bare claims name only the tool, which is exactly the pattern lesson two asked you to notice and fix.

prompt: Sequence the cleanup steps for a repo you're about to link on your portfolio, fastest safety issue first.

items: Remove any committed API keys or secrets
Rename unclear variables (x, data2, doStuff)
Write a short README
Do one full read-through as a stranger would

hints: Safety first, then the cheapest high-impact fix, then the thing most reviewers actually read, then a final check.
explanation: Secrets are a real risk, not a style choice, so they're removed first. Renaming is the cheapest fix that makes every later step easier. The README is what most reviewers actually read. The final read-through catches whatever's left.

prompt:
Given four candidate projects, which one should be left off a three-project portfolio, and why?

A: Finished, live, explains a decision, built 4 months ago.
B: A tutorial followed exactly with no changes, never deployed.
C: Finished, live, explains a decision, built last week.
D: Finished, live, explains a decision, built 7 months ago.

options.text: B — it fails 'explains a decision' since none were made, and it was never deployed
D — it's the oldest, so it should be cut for recency
A — it's the most average of the four, so it adds the least

hints: Apply the four criteria one at a time before comparing projects to each other.
explanation: B fails two of the four criteria outright — it isn't deployed and there's no decision to explain, since it's an unmodified tutorial. A, C, and D all pass all four criteria; 'oldest of three good options' isn't the same as 'fails a criterion,' and seven months is still reasonably recent.

prompt: Statement: an honest project description can still sound confident — honesty and confidence aren't in tension.

config.statement: An honest project description can still sound confident — honesty and confidence aren't in tension.
config.rubric: Should note that specific, checkable claims (this module's 'honest claim' category) are both true and confident — confidence doesn't require inflating the scope, and honesty doesn't require apologizing.

hints: Think back to the weather-app example with the offline cache — was that sentence modest, confident, or exaggerated?
explanation: The weather-app sentence from lesson three — 'caches the last successful response so it still shows something useful if the API is down' — is both fully honest and fully confident. It states a real, specific capability plainly, with no hedge and no inflation. The two qualities aren't opposites; undersell and oversell are the two failure modes either side of that honest, confident middle.

prompt: You need to find out, in a library's documentation, how to make a saved value survive a page refresh. The docs have these sections: Introduction, Installation, API Reference, Guides, Changelog, FAQ. Where do you look first?

options.text: Introduction, to understand the library's philosophy first
Guides — search for something like 'persistence' or 'storage' before reading any reference material
Changelog, to see the most recent updates
API Reference, read start to finish

hints: You have a specific task, not a general curiosity about the library — search for the task, don't read for context.
A Guides section usually exists precisely to answer 'how do I do X,' which is exactly your question.
explanation: Guides sections exist to answer task-shaped questions directly, which is exactly the shape of your question. The Introduction explains philosophy you don't need yet, the Changelog answers a different question entirely, and reading the full API reference start to finish to answer one task-shaped question is the slowest possible path to the answer, even though it will eventually contain it.

prompt: Statement: reading documentation top to bottom before writing any code is generally the fastest way to start using a new library.

config.statement: Reading documentation top to bottom before writing any code is generally the fastest way to start using a new library.
config.rubric: Should note that most documentation is a reference, not a narrative — reading it end to end front-loads information you don't need yet and delays the point where you're actually testing anything against real code.

hints: Think about how much of a typical docs site you'd actually use to build one small feature.
A reference is organized for lookup, not for a linear read — reading it like a book fights its own structure.
explanation: Most documentation is a reference organized for lookup — a quickstart, a set of guides, an API list — not a narrative meant to be read start to finish. Reading it end to end front-loads a large amount of information for features you may never touch, and delays the point where you're actually writing and testing real code, which is when documentation becomes genuinely useful instead of abstract.

prompt: You want to learn a new CSS framework. Which of these is the smallest *real* thing to build with it, in the sense this lesson means?

options.text: Follow the framework's official tutorial exactly, to the end
Rebuild one existing component from a project you already made, using only the new framework
Read the whole component library documentation before touching code
Start a brand-new large project using every feature of the framework

hints: 'Smallest real thing' means something you'll actually debug, not something someone else already debugged for you.
Rebuilding something familiar isolates what's different about the new tool, because you already know what the old version looked like.
explanation: Rebuilding one component you already understand isolates exactly what's new — the framework's syntax and conventions — without also having to invent what the component should do. A tutorial followed to the end teaches pattern-matching against the tutorial's exact steps, not debugging in the framework generally; reading a full library before touching code delays the point where you find out what you actually don't understand; a large new project introduces too many unknowns at once to tell which one caused a given problem.

prompt: You want to learn a backend framework you've never used. Pick one thing you've already built (in an earlier phase of this track, or elsewhere) and describe, in 2-3 sentences, the smallest real slice of it you could rebuild in the new framework to actually learn something.
hints: Name something specific and small — one endpoint, not a whole API.
Pick something you already know the correct behavior of, so you can tell when the new framework's version is wrong.
Avoid picking something so trivial it wouldn't exercise anything the framework actually does differently (e.g. a route that returns a static string).
explanation: A strong answer names one specific, previously-built piece of behavior — e.g. 'the endpoint that saves a new budget entry and returns the updated total' — rebuilt in the new framework. It's small enough to finish in an hour or two, but real enough to hit the framework's actual conventions for routing, request parsing, and a response, which is exactly what following a generic tutorial wouldn't teach as specifically.

prompt: Sort each reason for learning a new tool into 'solves a problem I actually have' or 'chasing the trend.'

categories: Solves a problem I actually have

items.text: My current app's state logic is genuinely tangled and hard to reason about, and this library is built to fix exactly that
items.category: Solves a problem I actually have

items.text: This framework was mentioned in three job postings I liked this week
I keep hand-writing the same validation logic and a library exists that does it in one line, tested
items.category: Solves a problem I actually have

items.text: A popular creator posted that everyone should be using this tool now
My deploys keep breaking in a way this specific tool is designed to catch before it ships
items.category: Solves a problem I actually have

hints: Ask: did I run into this problem myself, on my own project, before hearing about the tool?
'Everyone's using it' and 'it's in job postings' describe the tool's popularity, not your need for it.
explanation: The reliable test is sequence: did the problem exist for you before you heard about the tool, or did hearing about the tool create the sense that you had a problem? Popularity and job-posting frequency are real signals worth tracking generally, but they don't tell you whether learning the tool *right now* solves something you're actually stuck on — and learning driven by an actual stuck point sticks far better than learning driven by FOMO.

prompt: A learner's plan for the next month: Monday, start a GraphQL tutorial; Wednesday, switch to learning Rust after seeing a post about it; Friday, start a Docker course; the following Monday, none of the three finished, start a new one on a testing framework. What's the core flaw in this plan?

options.text: None of these four tools are worth learning
Nothing was chosen because of a problem the learner actually has right now — each switch was triggered by something external, not by hitting a wall
A month isn't enough time to learn even one of these properly
The order should have been Docker, then GraphQL, then Rust

hints: Look at what triggers each switch — is it 'I got stuck on X, and this solves X,' or something else?
The problem isn't the number of tools, it's what's driving the choice between them.
explanation: All four tools are genuinely useful in the right context — the flaw isn't the tools, it's that nothing in this plan was triggered by an actual obstacle in the learner's own work. Each switch happens because something else caught their attention, not because the previous tool stopped being useful or the new one solves a real blocker. A learning plan built entirely on external triggers produces exactly this pattern: four starts, zero finishes, no real depth in anything.

prompt: Match each scenario to whether a framework is likely worth adopting for it.

pairs.left: A single-page tool with one form and no routing
pairs.right: Probably not worth it — the framework's overhead likely exceeds what one simple screen needs

pairs.left: An app with six interacting views that all need to share and update the same data
pairs.right: Probably worth it — shared state across many views is exactly what a framework's conventions are built to manage

pairs.left: A marketing landing page with no interactivity beyond a contact form
pairs.right: Probably not worth it — plain HTML and a small amount of JS will out-simplify a framework here

hints: Ask what the framework actually buys for this specific app's shape, not in general.
Complexity that isn't there yet is a cost with no matching benefit.
explanation: A framework earns its cost when an app's actual complexity — shared state, many interacting views, frequent re-renders — matches what the framework exists to manage. A one-form tool or a mostly-static page doesn't have that complexity yet, so the framework's build step, bundle size, and learning curve are a pure cost with nothing to offset them.

prompt: You're building a to-do app with three views (list, add, settings) that all read and update the same list of tasks. A friend says 'just use vanilla JS, frameworks are overkill for something this small.' In 2-3 sentences, say whether you agree, and why, using this lesson's cost/benefit framing.
hints: Three interacting views sharing the same data is closer to the 'framework helps' end than the 'one form' end — weigh it against that, not against 'is this technically small.'
It's fine to disagree with the friend if you can name the specific complexity (shared state across views) that justifies it.
explanation: A strong answer notices that 'small' isn't the same test as 'simple' — three views that all read and write the same task list is exactly the kind of shared-state complexity a framework is built to manage, even in an app with few total files. The friend's advice is a reasonable default for a genuinely single-view tool, but doesn't hold once multiple views need to stay in sync with the same data.

prompt: Statement: watching one more tutorial before starting your own project is usually the right call if you're not sure you understand the tool well enough yet.

config.statement: Watching one more tutorial before starting your own project is usually the right call if you're not sure you understand the tool well enough yet.
config.rubric: Should note that 'not sure I understand it' is often resolved faster by attempting something and finding the specific gap than by consuming more general material, and that 'one more tutorial' is a common form of avoidance that feels like productive preparation.

hints: What actually tells you whether you understand something — reading about it again, or trying to use it and seeing exactly where it breaks?
Notice the pattern: is this the first tutorial, or the fourth on the same topic?
explanation: If it's the first exposure to a genuinely new concept, one more tutorial can be exactly right. But 'not sure I understand it well enough' after several tutorials is usually resolved faster by attempting something real and finding the *specific* gap — which tutorial-watching, by its nature, can't reveal, because someone else already made every decision. 'One more tutorial' is one of the most common and comfortable forms this avoidance takes, precisely because it feels like productive preparation instead of stalling.

prompt: Which of these is the clearer sign that you know enough of a new tool to start building with it, rather than needing more preparation first?

options.text: You could recite the tool's full feature list from memory
You can build a small, broken version of something and have a rough idea where to look when it breaks
You've read every page of the documentation once
You feel fully confident and no longer nervous about starting

hints: The bar isn't comprehensive knowledge — it's whether you can generate and then interpret an error.
Confidence and actual readiness aren't the same thing, in either direction.
explanation: 'Can build something small and broken, with a rough idea where to look when it fails' is the readiness signal that actually predicts whether independent building will go well — it means you have a real, if incomplete, mental model of the tool. Reciting features or having read every page are both forms of passive familiarity that don't test whether you can *use* the tool; waiting for full confidence is waiting for a feeling that, for most people learning something new, arrives during building, not before it.

prompt: You need to know what arguments a specific function takes, and you already know its name. Which doc section do you go to?

options.text: API Reference — search for the function name directly
Introduction
Guides

hints: You already know the function's name — this is exactly what a reference is built to look up.
explanation: Once you know the function's name, the API Reference is the fastest path — this is what reference documentation is for, distinct from the task-oriented Guides section used in lesson one's other example.

prompt: Scope the smallest real slice for: learning a new form-validation library, when you've already built a signup form by hand before.
hints: Reuse a form you've already built and know the correct validation rules for.
explanation: A strong answer rebuilds the validation logic of the already-built signup form using the new library — small, finishable, and testable against behavior you already know is correct.

prompt: Sort each learning trigger.

items.text: A recurring bug that a specific tool would have caught
A tool mentioned in a newsletter this morning
Your project outgrew what your current approach can manage
Someone you follow said it's the future of the field

hints: Ask whether the problem existed before the tool was mentioned, or after.
explanation: The genuine-need items describe a problem in the learner's own project preceding the tool. The external-trigger items describe hearing about the tool with no matching problem yet identified.

prompt: A project is a single settings page with three toggles and no shared state with anything else. Is a framework likely worth adopting?

config.statement: A framework is likely worth adopting for a single settings page with three toggles and no shared state.
config.rubric: Should note the absence of shared state across views — the specific complexity a framework helps manage — as the reason it isn't worth it here.

hints: What complexity does a framework actually solve, and is it present in a three-toggle single page?
explanation: No shared state across multiple views means none of a framework's core benefit applies here — the build step and learning curve would be pure cost for a page this simple.

prompt: A doc page's code example looks like it will work, but a warning box says the function is asynchronous and returns a promise. What's the risk of skipping the warning box?

options.text: None — the code example alone is always sufficient
Code that assumes a synchronous return value will silently use an unresolved promise instead of the real result
The page will just look less polished

hints: Think about what happens if code expects a value immediately, but actually gets a promise.
explanation: Treating a promise as if it were already resolved produces a bug that often doesn't throw an obvious error — it just silently uses the wrong value, which is exactly the kind of caveat warning boxes exist to flag before it costs an afternoon of debugging.

prompt: A learner has read the full docs for a tool twice but hasn't tried building anything with it, saying they want to be 'completely sure' first. Genuine preparation, or avoidance?

options.text: Genuine preparation — reading twice is thorough, not excessive
Likely avoidance — reading can't produce a visible failure, and 'completely sure' isn't a testable bar
Impossible to tell without knowing the tool

hints: 'Completely sure' is a feeling with no test attached to it — compare it to the concrete readiness signal from lesson five.
explanation: 'Completely sure' has no concrete test, unlike 'can build something small and broken and know roughly where to look when it fails.' Reading the same material twice without attempting anything fits the avoidance pattern from lesson five closely.

prompt: Sequence these four in the order they typically happen for someone learning a new tool.

items: See the tool's basic shape via one introduction
Build something small and broken
Debug a specific real error using the docs
Feel meaningfully more confident

hints: Confidence tends to be the outcome of debugging, not a precondition for attempting it.
explanation: Confidence is downstream of the debugging step for most learners, not a gate that has to be passed before attempting it — waiting for it first tends to just delay the step that produces it.

prompt: Two pull request titles for the same change: A) 'fixed stuff', B) 'Fix cart total not updating when an item is removed'. What does title B do that title A doesn't?

options.text: It's longer, which always looks more thorough
It tells a reviewer what to check for without opening the diff
It uses more technical vocabulary
It includes the file names that changed

hints: What could a reviewer do with title A before opening the diff? What about title B?
A good title lets someone decide whether and how urgently to review before they've looked at any code.
explanation: Title B names the specific bug and its trigger — a reviewer instantly knows what behavior to test for, without opening a single file. Title A requires opening the diff and reading every changed line just to find out what 'stuff' meant, which is exactly the extra work a good title exists to remove. Length and vocabulary aren't the point — specificity about the actual change is.

prompt: Statement: a pull request that changes twelve unrelated things at once is generally easier to review than five small pull requests, one per change.

config.statement: A pull request that changes twelve unrelated things at once is generally easier to review than five small pull requests, one per change.
config.rubric: Should note that a reviewer can hold a small, scoped diff in their head and reason about it, while a large mixed diff forces them to track many unrelated changes at once, making real review much harder and slower.

hints: Think about how much a reviewer has to hold in their head at once for each kind of PR.
A small diff can usually be understood completely. A large mixed one usually can't be, in one sitting.
explanation: A small, scoped diff can be held in a reviewer's head completely — they can reason about every line and be confident they understood the whole change. A large diff mixing twelve unrelated things forces a reviewer to either skim (missing real problems) or spend far longer than the sum of five smaller reviews would have taken. Size isn't neutral — it changes what kind of review is actually possible.

prompt: A review comment reads: 'This will break if the cart is empty — you're calling `.reduce()` with no initial value.' Which response best separates the feedback from your sense of yourself as a programmer?

options.text: 'You're right, I missed the empty-cart case — I'll add an initial value.'
'Sorry, I'm still learning, I know this probably wasn't good enough.'
Not responding, and quietly fixing it without saying anything
'It works fine on my machine.'

hints: The strongest response treats the comment as information about the code, not a verdict on the author.
Apologizing for your general skill level responds to a feeling the comment didn't actually express.
explanation: The first response engages with exactly what the comment said — a specific, missed edge case — and states the fix, nothing more and nothing less. The apology response responds to a judgment about the author's overall skill that the comment never made; it turns a one-line technical note into a referendum on competence. Silent fixing avoids the discomfort but also avoids confirming to the reviewer that the point landed, which erodes trust in a way that costs more than a short reply would have.

prompt: Describe, in 2-3 sentences, the difference between 'this code has a bug' and 'I am bad at this' — and one concrete thing you could say to yourself, in the moment a review comment lands, to keep the two apart.
hints: Name the actual distinction: code is a thing you made, separate from your overall ability, and a specific bug is evidence about one piece of code, not a general verdict.
A concrete self-statement is something short and specific, not a vague reassurance.
explanation: A strong answer names that a bug describes one specific, fixable fact about a piece of code at one point in time, while 'I am bad at this' is a global claim about identity that the comment never actually made — the gap between them is manufactured by the reader, not supplied by the reviewer. A concrete self-statement might be something like 'this is one line, not my whole codebase' or 'they found this because they're reviewing carefully, which is the review working, not me failing.'

prompt: Which review comment is both kind and useful?

options.text: 'This is wrong.'
'This breaks if `items` is empty — `items[0]` will be undefined. Might be worth an early return or a default value here.'
'Not sure I'd have done it this way, but whatever works I guess.'
'Great job! 😊'

hints: A useful comment names the specific problem and a specific direction, without being harsh.
Praise with no content and criticism with no content are both, in different ways, unactionable.
explanation: The second comment names the exact condition that breaks (empty `items`), the specific consequence (`items[0]` is undefined), and a concrete direction to consider — all without any harshness. 'This is wrong' is harsh with no information; 'whatever works I guess' hides real doubt behind false permissiveness, which is its own kind of unhelpful; 'Great job!' with no content teaches the author nothing, even though it's kind.

prompt: Rewrite this review comment to be specific, actionable, and kind: 'nit: this is kind of messy, might want to clean it up.' The actual issue: a function is 40 lines long and does three unrelated things (validates input, saves to a database, and sends an email).
hints: Name the actual issue (three unrelated responsibilities in one function), not just 'messy.'
Suggest a specific direction (e.g. splitting into three functions) rather than leaving 'clean it up' undefined.
It's fine to soften the tone with a question or a 'worth considering' — that's kindness, not vagueness, as long as the content is specific.
explanation: A strong rewrite names the real issue and a specific direction: 'This function validates input, saves to the database, and sends an email — might be worth splitting into three smaller functions so each one's easier to test and reuse on its own. Not blocking, just worth considering.' It replaces 'messy' with the actual reason it's hard to follow, and replaces 'clean it up' with something the author can act on directly.

prompt: Two issues on an open source repo: A) 'Add full dark mode support across the entire app, with theming, animations, and user preferences,' labeled 'help wanted.' B) 'Typo in README: "recieve" should be "receive",' labeled 'good first issue.' Which is the better first contribution to attempt?

options.text: A — bigger contributions make a stronger impression
B — small, scoped, clearly labeled for newcomers, low risk of stalling out
Either — size doesn't matter for a first contribution

hints: 'good first issue' is a real, deliberate label maintainers use — it's worth taking at face value.
A first contribution's job is to learn the actual process (fork, PR, review, merge), not to prove maximum skill immediately.
explanation: Issue B is explicitly labeled for newcomers, tiny in scope, and nearly impossible to get wrong — which makes it ideal for learning the actual mechanics of contributing (fork, branch, PR, review, merge) without the risk of stalling on a large, ambiguous feature with no clear finish line. Issue A is a genuinely valuable contribution for someone already familiar with the project's codebase and conventions — not a good first move.

prompt: Put these steps of a first open source contribution in order.

items: Read the project's CONTRIBUTING.md file
Comment on the issue to say you're working on it
Fork the repo and make a small, scoped change
Open a pull request referencing the issue, with a clear description
Respond to review feedback and update the PR

hints: CONTRIBUTING.md often states exactly what maintainers expect — skipping it is a common way to waste a maintainer's time.
Claiming an issue before starting prevents two people from duplicating the same work.
explanation: Reading CONTRIBUTING.md first avoids doing something the maintainers explicitly ask contributors not to do — many projects have their own conventions for commit messages, testing, or issue etiquette. Commenting to claim the issue prevents wasted, duplicate work. Then the actual change, then the PR, then — almost always — a round of review feedback to respond to, since a first contribution rarely merges on the first try, which is entirely normal.

prompt: Which async status update needs the fewest follow-up questions to act on?

options.text: 'Working on the login stuff, will update soon.'
'Login form validation is done and tested. Next: connecting it to the auth API — blocked on knowing which error codes it returns, can someone confirm before I continue?'
'Made some progress today.'

hints: A self-contained update states what's done, what's next, and names any blocker explicitly.
'Soon' and 'some progress' both require a follow-up question to become actionable.
explanation: The second update states exactly what's finished, what's next, and names a specific blocker with a specific question attached — a teammate can act on it immediately, with no back-and-forth required first. The other two both require at least one follow-up question just to find out what's actually going on, which is precisely the round-trip async communication is meant to avoid.

prompt: Write a self-contained async check-in message for this situation: you finished the cart page yesterday, started the checkout flow today but hit an error you don't understand yet involving a payment library's callback, and you're not sure when you'll have capacity to dig into it further this week.
hints: State what's done, what's in progress, and name the specific blocker rather than a vague 'stuck.'
It's fine and honest to name uncertain capacity without over-explaining or apologizing for it.
A good message needs no reply to be useful — someone should be able to read it and know exactly where things stand.
explanation: A strong message states all three things plainly: cart page done, checkout flow started, blocked on a specific payment-library callback error (named, even if not yet understood), and an honest, non-apologetic note about uncertain capacity this week — e.g. 'may not get back to this until later in the week depending on how I'm doing.' A teammate reading it knows exactly where things stand without needing to ask anything.

prompt: Which pull request title is reviewable at a glance?

options.text: 'updates'
'Fix checkout button staying disabled after a failed payment attempt'
'small change'

hints: Look for a title that tells you what to test without opening the diff.
explanation: The second title names the specific behavior fixed, letting a reviewer know exactly what to check before opening a single file — the other two require opening the diff just to find out what changed.

prompt: Rewrite this comment to be specific and actionable: 'this function could probably be better.' The actual issue: the function has no error handling around a network call, so a failed request crashes the page.
hints: Name the actual missing behavior (error handling) and its consequence (the crash), not just 'could be better.'
explanation: A strong rewrite names the real gap and its effect: 'This network call has no error handling — if it fails, the page currently crashes. Worth wrapping in a try/catch and showing a fallback message?' Specific problem, specific direction, delivered as a question.

prompt: Sort each internal reaction to a review comment.

categories: Reacting to a judgment the comment didn't make

items.text: 'Good catch, I missed that case, fixing it now'
'I clearly shouldn't be doing this'
items.category: Reacting to a judgment the comment didn't make

items.text: 'That's a fair point about the edge case, let me address it'
'They must think I'm incompetent'
items.category: Reacting to a judgment the comment didn't make

hints: Ask whether the reaction responds to what the comment actually said, or to a feeling about the self it never stated.
explanation: The engaging-with-the-code reactions respond to the actual technical content. The other two respond to a global judgment about ability that the original comments never made.

prompt: Which of these is the better first open source contribution?

options.text: A labeled 'good first issue': fix a broken link in the docs
An unlabeled issue proposing a major architecture rewrite

hints: Take the 'good first issue' label at face value — it's a deliberate signal.
explanation: The labeled issue is small, scoped, and explicitly meant for newcomers — ideal for learning the contribution process itself. A major rewrite proposal is a poor first attempt regardless of skill level.

prompt: Sequence these four steps of a first contribution.

items: Comment on the issue to claim it
Read CONTRIBUTING.md
Make the change and open a PR
Respond to review feedback

hints: CONTRIBUTING.md often comes before even claiming the issue, since it may state how to do exactly that.
explanation: CONTRIBUTING.md is read first since it often states the expected process for even claiming an issue; then the issue is claimed to avoid duplicate work; then the change and PR; then, almost always, a round of feedback.

prompt: Statement: 'Made some progress today, will keep you posted' is a self-contained async update.

config.statement: 'Made some progress today, will keep you posted' is a self-contained async update.
config.rubric: Should note it states neither what's done nor what's next nor any specific blocker, requiring a follow-up question to become actionable.

hints: Could a teammate act on this without asking a follow-up question?
explanation: It states nothing specific — not what's done, not what's next, not any blocker — so a teammate has no way to act on it without a follow-up question, which defeats the purpose of an async update.

prompt: Which sentence names uncertain capacity professionally, without oversharing?

options.text: 'May not get to this until later in the week, depending on how the week goes.'
A detailed explanation of a specific health condition and its symptoms
No mention of timing at all, leaving the teammate to assume a normal pace

hints: The useful boundary states the practical fact without the private reason behind it.
explanation: The first option states a plain, practical, professional fact a teammate can plan around. The second overshares private information nobody asked for and isn't owed. The third leaves a teammate planning around an assumption that may turn out to be wrong.

prompt: Match each route to its honest, primary trade-off.

pairs.right: Steadiest income and the least schedule flexibility — fixed hours and an interview process to get in
The most schedule flexibility, attractive for variable energy, but income is unpredictable and you also have to find the work

pairs.left: Product (building your own thing to sell)
pairs.right: Highest potential upside, but the slowest to any income and the highest chance of never reaching it

hints: Think about what each route trades for what, not which one is 'best' in the abstract.
Flexibility, stability, and upside potential are three different axes — no route wins on all three at once.
explanation: None of the three routes dominates the others — each buys something real at a real cost. Employment buys stability at the cost of fixed hours and a competitive hiring process. Freelance buys schedule control at the cost of income predictability and the extra, ongoing work of finding clients. Product work buys the largest possible upside at the cost of the longest timeline to any income at all, with a real chance of never reaching it. The right route depends on which trade-off you can actually live with right now, not which sounds best.

prompt: Statement: freelance work is the obviously best route for someone managing variable energy, since it offers the most schedule flexibility.

config.statement: Freelance work is the obviously best route for someone managing variable energy, since it offers the most schedule flexibility.
config.rubric: Should note that flexibility is real but comes with income unpredictability and the extra work of finding clients, which can itself be a significant, unpredictable energy cost — 'best' depends on which trade-off is more manageable, not on flexibility alone.

hints: Flexibility is one real benefit — but what does freelance cost in exchange, and is that cost also energy-relevant?
Finding freelance work is itself an ongoing task, not a one-time setup — does that fit variable capacity better or worse than a fixed job search once?
explanation: Schedule flexibility is real, but freelance also trades away income stability and adds an ongoing task — finding and maintaining client relationships — that itself costs energy unpredictably. For some people at variable capacity that trade is worth it; for others, the stability and one-time (rather than continuous) job search of employment is the better fit. Neither route is obviously best in general — it depends on which specific trade-off is more sustainable for a given person's actual pattern of good and bad periods.

prompt: A junior developer job posting lists: '5+ years React experience, expert in Kubernetes, PhD preferred.' The role is genuinely entry-level and pays accordingly. What's the most likely explanation?

options.text: The posting is accurate and you should not apply without meeting every line
The list is inflated — often written as an aspirational wishlist or copy-pasted from a senior template, not a hard bar
The company made a typo and meant to write 'junior' as 'senior'

hints: Compare the stated requirements to what the role is actually paying and calling itself — does the mismatch make sense if the list were literal?
This is an extremely common, well-documented pattern in hiring, not a one-off error.
explanation: An entry-level title and salary paired with a senior-level requirements list is a well-known mismatch — postings are frequently written by someone compiling a wishlist of every skill that would be nice to have, or reusing a template from a more senior role, rather than reflecting what's actually required to be considered. Taking the list as a literal hard bar filters out qualified junior candidates, including ones who would otherwise apply.

prompt: A posting for a junior role lists 'strong communication skills, team player, experience with agile methodologies, familiarity with CI/CD, bachelor's degree or equivalent experience.' In 2-3 sentences, say which of these you'd treat as a likely hard requirement and which as a soft wishlist item, and why.
hints: 'Bachelor's degree or equivalent experience' explicitly offers an alternative path — that's a signal it's softer than it looks.
Vague, unmeasurable phrases like 'team player' and 'strong communication' are almost never hard-screened on their own.
Specific tool/process familiarity (CI/CD, agile) for a junior role is more plausibly a real, if soft, preference than a hard bar.
explanation: A strong answer notices that 'bachelor's degree or equivalent experience' names its own escape hatch, which is a real signal it's a soft preference; 'strong communication' and 'team player' are unmeasurable phrases that almost every posting includes and that almost never actually gate a junior candidate on their own. Familiarity with CI/CD or agile is plausible as a genuine (if soft) preference for a junior role, since it's concrete enough to actually assess, but rarely a hard bar for an entry-level position.

prompt: Sequence these steps from a vague first client ask to a scoped, priced deliverable.

items: Client says: 'Can you fix my website, it's kind of broken'
Ask specific questions: broken how, on what page, since when
Narrow it to one concrete, checkable task (e.g. 'the contact form doesn't send an email on submit')
State the scope and price back to the client before starting: 'I'll fix the contact form not sending emails, for $X, and confirm it's working before you pay'
Do the scoped work and confirm the fix against the original complaint

hints: A vague ask has to be narrowed into something checkable before a price makes sense.
Confirming scope and price back to the client, before starting, is what prevents a small job quietly growing into a large unpaid one.
explanation: Turning 'kind of broken' into 'the contact form doesn't send an email on submit' is the actual work of scoping — everything before that step is too vague to price honestly. Stating the scope and price back to the client, before starting, is what prevents scope creep — without it, 'fix my website' can quietly expand to include anything the client later decides is also broken.

prompt: A friend of a friend messages: 'my small bakery's website is old and I want it updated, can you help?' Write 2-3 sentences of the clarifying questions you'd ask to turn this into a scoped, priceable task.
hints: Ask about what specifically is wrong or wanted (design, content, a broken feature, mobile-friendliness), not just 'updated.'
Ask about a rough budget or what 'updated' would need to include to count as done, to avoid scoping something the client can't actually afford.
It's fine to ask more than one question — the goal is to leave with something checkable, not a single perfect question.
explanation: A strong set of questions narrows the vague ask along multiple concrete axes: what specifically feels outdated (the design, the content, that it's not mobile-friendly?), what would make it feel 'done,' and roughly what budget or timeline they have in mind. The goal of all of them is the same: turning 'updated' into something specific enough to scope and price honestly, the same move as the contact-form example.

prompt: Sort each situation into the pricing model it fits better: hourly or flat fee.

items.text: The scope is genuinely unclear and might expand as you investigate
A tightly scoped, well-understood task like the contact-form fix from lesson three
You expect a crash or bad week might extend the timeline unpredictably
The client wants cost certainty upfront for a small, bounded task

hints: Hourly protects you when scope or time is uncertain. Flat fee is fine when scope is genuinely well-defined and small.
Think about who bears the risk of the job taking longer than expected under each model.
explanation: Hourly billing shifts the risk of an uncertain or expanding scope, or an unpredictable timeline, onto the client in a transparent way — you're paid for the time actually spent, whatever that turns out to be. Flat fee shifts that same risk onto you, which is fine and often preferred by clients when the scope is genuinely small and well understood, but risky when either the task or your own week could turn out to be longer than expected.

prompt: You're pricing the contact-form fix from lesson three — a single, well-scoped bug in a small business's site, expected to take roughly one to two hours. State a price and briefly justify it using this lesson's framing (not a specific dollar figure you're told to hit — reason about a fair range).
hints: Reason from an hourly rate you'd consider fair for your current skill level, multiplied by the estimated time, with some cushion for the scope being flat-fee (which shifts risk to you).
It's fine to price modestly for a genuinely first paid job — the goal here is a defensible, honest number, not the highest possible one.
explanation: A strong answer reasons explicitly: an hourly rate considered fair for a beginner (commonly landing somewhere in a modest range depending on region and market), times the estimated one to two hours, plus a small cushion since it's a flat fee and any underestimate becomes the freelancer's cost rather than the client's. The specific number matters less than showing the reasoning — starting from time and rate, not from a number picked out of the air.

prompt: Which sentence names variable capacity to a client professionally, without oversharing?

options.text: 'My turnaround time can vary week to week — I'll always flag it early if a deadline needs adjusting.'
A full explanation of a specific diagnosis and its symptoms
No mention of timing at all, and hoping it doesn't come up

hints: The useful version states a practical, plannable fact — variable turnaround — without the private reason behind it.
Silence isn't neutral here — it leaves a client planning around an assumption of consistent turnaround that may not hold.
explanation: The first sentence states exactly what a client needs in order to plan: turnaround may vary, and they'll be told early if that affects a deadline. It requires no medical detail to be complete and professional. Full disclosure overshares information nobody asked for and isn't owed; silence leaves the client planning around an assumption that may turn out to be false, which tends to damage trust more than a plain, early heads-up would have.

prompt: Write the sentence or two you'd actually put in a freelance agreement or an early email with a new client, naming that your availability and turnaround can vary, without disclosing a diagnosis or specific symptoms.
hints: State the practical fact (variable turnaround, will flag early) without the private reason.
Keep it brief and matter-of-fact — this doesn't need justification or apology to be complete.
explanation: A strong answer is short and practical: something like 'My schedule can vary week to week; if a deadline is at risk I'll flag it as early as possible so we can adjust together.' It states a plannable fact plainly, requires no explanation of why, and reads as professional rather than apologetic — matching the honest-not-modest register from earlier in this phase.

prompt: A person needs steady, predictable income within six weeks and can tolerate a fixed application process. Which route best fits, on the trade-offs from this module alone?

options.text: Employed
Product
Freelance

hints: Match the stated constraint (steady income, six-week timeline) against each route's real trade-off.
explanation: Employment's trade-off — a fixed process for the most predictable income — is the closest match to this specific constraint set; product work's slow timeline is a poor fit for a six-week need.

prompt: Sort each line from a junior posting.

items.text: 'Team player, passionate about technology'
'Bachelor's degree or equivalent experience'
'Must be legally authorized to work in this country'
'5+ years experience' on a role titled and paid as entry-level

hints: Legal/eligibility requirements are categorically different from skill wishlist items — they're rarely negotiable.
explanation: Vague personality phrases and mismatched experience requirements on an entry-level posting are classic wishlist signals. A legal work-authorization requirement is a different category entirely — a real, non-negotiable bar.

prompt: Turn this into a scoped task: 'my app crashes sometimes.' Name the single next clarifying question you'd ask.
hints: The question should narrow 'sometimes' toward a specific, reproducible condition.
explanation: A strong question narrows toward reproducibility: 'When does it crash — on a specific screen, after a specific action, or does it seem random?' This is the same move as the contact-form example: turning vague into checkable.

prompt: A job's scope is 'redesign my whole site, not sure exactly what I want yet, let's figure it out as we go.' Which pricing model fits?

options.text: Hourly — the scope is explicitly not yet defined
Flat fee — it's simpler for the client

hints: A flat fee is a bet on a known scope. Is the scope here known?
explanation: The client has explicitly said the scope isn't defined yet — a flat fee here would mean betting on an unknown, which is exactly the situation hourly billing is meant to handle fairly.

prompt: Estimate a flat fee for a task expected to take 2 hours at a chosen fair hourly rate, including a cushion for the flat-fee risk. Show your reasoning.
hints: State the rate, multiply by the estimated hours, then add a cushion and explain why.
explanation: A strong answer reasons explicitly: rate × 2 hours, plus roughly 20-30% cushion, because flat fee shifts the risk of the job running long onto the freelancer, and the cushion is the price of taking on that risk.

prompt: Which of these correctly names variable capacity to a client?

options.text: 'Turnaround may vary week to week — I'll flag early if it affects a deadline.'
A detailed account of a specific chronic illness diagnosis
Saying nothing and hoping it's fine

hints: The professional version states a plannable fact, no more and no less.
explanation: The first option is the complete, professional version — a plannable fact with a commitment to early communication, nothing more.

prompt: Statement: saying nothing about variable turnaround is a neutral, safe default.

config.statement: Saying nothing about variable turnaround is a neutral, safe default.
config.rubric: Should note that silence leaves a client planning around an assumption of consistent turnaround, which tends to damage trust more than an early, plain heads-up would.

hints: What does the client assume by default if nothing is said, and what happens if that assumption turns out wrong?
explanation: Silence isn't neutral — it leaves the client planning around an unstated assumption of consistent turnaround, and that assumption breaking without warning tends to cost more trust than a plain, early statement would have.

prompt: Sequence the safe steps for resuming a project you haven't touched in a month.

items: Read your own README or notes on what the project does and where you left off
Try to run it exactly as-is, without changing anything yet
If it fails, diagnose the specific failure (dependency version, missing env var, etc.) rather than assuming you forgot everything
Fix only that specific failure
Resume the actual work you meant to do before the gap

hints: Reading your own notes first re-orients you faster than diving straight into code.
Running it unchanged first tells you whether the problem is the project or your memory of it.
explanation: Reading your own notes re-establishes context before touching anything. Running it unchanged first isolates whether there's an actual technical problem (rather than guessing and changing things at random). Diagnosing the specific failure — rather than assuming a vague, global 'I forgot everything' — usually reveals a narrow, fixable cause like a dependency drift or a missing environment variable. Only then does the original work resume, on a project that's actually confirmed to run again.

prompt: Statement: if a project won't run after a month away, the most likely explanation is that you've forgotten how the code works.

config.statement: If a project won't run after a month away, the most likely explanation is that you've forgotten how the code works.
config.rubric: Should note that a project failing to run after a gap is very often a mechanical drift issue (dependency updates, a changed Node version, an expired local env var) rather than a comprehension issue, and these two have very different, specific fixes.

hints: A project can fail to *run* for reasons that have nothing to do with whether you still understand the code.
What actually changes on a machine over a month, even if the project's code doesn't change at all?
explanation: 'Won't run' and 'I don't understand it anymore' are usually two different problems with two different causes. Over a month, dependencies get updated, a system's installed language version can shift, and local environment variables or config files can be lost or expire — none of which has anything to do with comprehension. Treating a 'won't run' error as evidence of forgotten understanding often leads to a much scarier, slower response (rereading everything) than the actual fix (checking dependency versions) requires.

prompt: Which single addition to a project's README would help future-you the most after a long gap?

options.text: A longer list of every technology used
A short note on what you were doing when you last stopped, and what the next step was going to be
A more detailed license section
More inline code comments throughout every file

hints: Think about the specific question future-you will actually be asking on day one back: not 'what does this project do' but 'where exactly did I leave off.'
Setup steps and tech lists answer 'what is this.' Only one of the options answers 'where was I.'
explanation: The specific gap a returning developer hits first isn't usually 'what is this project' — that's answerable from the rest of the README — it's 'what was I in the middle of.' A short note naming the exact last state and next intended step answers exactly that question, which nothing else on the list does as directly.

prompt: Write the 'where I left off' note you'd want waiting for you in a project's README, for this situation: you'd just finished the login form's validation, and were about to start wiring it up to an actual auth check, but hadn't started yet.
hints: Name specifically what's done and what the very next concrete step was going to be.
Keep it short — a few sentences is enough, this isn't a full project history.
explanation: A strong note is short and specific: 'Login form validation is done and tested. Next step: wire the submit handler up to an actual auth check — haven't started this part yet. The validation logic is in LoginForm.jsx, lines ~40-70.' It answers exactly what a returning developer needs first: what's finished, and precisely where the next piece of work begins.

prompt: Sort each comparison habit.

items.text: Comparing this month's work to your own three months ago
Comparing your unfinished project to a stranger's polished, finished launch post online
Noticing a specific technique someone else's finished project used well, and studying that one technique
Comparing your pace, in general, to people who post daily and appear to have full-time hours to give this

hints: A useful comparison has a fair baseline — your own past, or a specific technique — not a stranger's edited highlight reel.
Ask whether the comparison gives you something actionable, or just a feeling of falling behind with nothing to do about it.
explanation: The useful comparisons share a fair baseline: your own trajectory, which accounts for your actual constraints, or one specific technique worth learning from, which is actionable. The corrosive comparisons share an unfair baseline: a finished, edited presentation of someone else's work (which hides their own messy middle), or a general pace comparison against people whose actual hours and constraints are invisible and probably very different from yours.

prompt: Describe, in 2-3 sentences, what you'd say to yourself the next time you catch yourself comparing your current, unfinished progress to someone else's polished, finished highlight-reel post — using this lesson's reframe.
hints: Name the actual mismatch being compared: your messy middle versus their edited end.
Offer a concrete redirect — e.g. comparing to your own past self instead — not just 'stop comparing.'
explanation: A strong answer names the specific mismatch — you're seeing your unfinished, in-progress work next to someone else's finished, edited presentation of theirs, which was never a fair comparison to begin with — and redirects to something actionable, like checking in against your own work from a few months ago instead. 'Just stop comparing' isn't actually usable advice; naming the specific distortion and having a concrete alternative comparison is.

prompt: For someone with genuinely low, unpredictable energy, which is the lower-energy way to find people to learn alongside?

options.text: A weekly scheduled live video meetup
An async text-based community (forum or chat) where you can post and reply whenever you have capacity
Attending a large in-person conference

hints: Async, text-based options remove the fixed-time and physical-presence costs that the other two require.
The goal is connection that fits your actual capacity pattern, not the option that looks most 'serious.'
explanation: An async, text-based community removes both the fixed-time cost (you engage whenever you actually have capacity, not at a scheduled hour) and the physical/audio-visual cost (no camera, no live conversation stamina required) that a live meetup or an in-person conference both demand. This isn't about one option being more 'real' community than another — it's about which one is actually sustainable to keep showing up to.

prompt: Write the first message you'd post introducing yourself in a new async learning community — 2-3 sentences, specific enough to invite a real reply rather than being generic.
hints: Name something specific you're currently working on or stuck on, not just 'hi, I'm new here.'
A specific, small detail (what you're learning, one thing you're currently stuck on) gives someone a concrete reason and way to reply.
explanation: A strong first message names something specific: 'Hi, I'm working through a fundamentals track, just finished a small budget tracker and I'm currently stuck on async state updates in vanilla JS — would love to hear how other people here have approached that.' A generic 'hi, excited to be here' gives nobody anything concrete to respond to; a specific detail — what you're building, what you're stuck on — is what actually invites a real reply.

prompt: Sort each piece of self-advice.

items.text: Believe in yourself and never give up
A project failing to run after a gap is almost always drift, not forgetting — check dependency versions before rereading the whole codebase
You've got this!
Write down where you stopped before you close the laptop — it takes thirty seconds and saves hours later

hints: A useful piece of advice is specific enough to actually act on the next time the situation arises.
Ask: could you literally do something different tomorrow because of this advice, or does it just feel encouraging?
explanation: The concrete pieces of advice each name a specific situation and a specific, actionable response — they're things a learner could literally do differently tomorrow. The platitudes are true in some general sense but give no specific action to take, in any particular situation — they feel encouraging without actually changing what happens next.

prompt: Write one piece of advice you'd give your own lesson-one self — concrete and specific enough that it names an actual situation and what to do about it, not a general encouragement.
hints: Ground it in something specific from your own actual experience across this track, not a generic statement anyone could write.
Test it: could you literally act differently tomorrow because of this, or does it just sound nice?
explanation: There's no single correct answer here — the bar is specificity, not content. A strong answer names a real situation (e.g. 'a tutorial hell you actually fell into,' 'a specific comparison that used to derail you') and a concrete response to it, in the same shape as this module's other worked examples — not a general 'believe in yourself,' which could be written by someone who'd never touched a line of code.

prompt: A project fails on startup with an error naming a specific outdated package version. Drift, or forgotten understanding?

options.text: Drift — the error names a specific mechanical cause
Forgotten understanding — reread the whole codebase first

hints: A specific error naming a version mismatch is a mechanical clue, not a comprehension one.
explanation: A specific version-mismatch error is a clear drift signal, unrelated to whether the learner still understands the code — the fix is checking that dependency, not rereading everything.

prompt: Write a 'where I left off' note for: you'd finished a recipe app's search feature and were about to start on saving favorites, hadn't begun that part.
hints: State what's done, what's next specifically, and that the next part hasn't been started.
explanation: A strong note: 'Search feature done and working. Next: saving favorites — haven't started this part yet.' Specific, short, and answers exactly what a returning developer needs first.

prompt: Sort each.

items.text: This month's progress versus your own progress six months ago
Your half-finished side project versus a stranger's polished portfolio launch
One specific technique in someone's finished project, studied on its own
Your overall pace versus people who appear to code full-time

hints: A fair comparison shares a baseline — your own past, or one isolated technique — not a stranger's edited whole.
explanation: The fair comparisons share a baseline that accounts for real constraints — your own past, or one specific technique in isolation. The unfair ones compare your visible, in-progress state to someone else's finished, curated presentation.

prompt: Rank by energy cost to sustain: async text forum, weekly live call, in-person meetup. Which is lowest?

options.text: Async text forum
Weekly live call
In-person meetup

hints: Async removes both the fixed-time cost and the physical/audio-visual cost the other two require.
explanation: Async, text-based participation has no fixed-time requirement and no physical or audio/video demand, making it the lowest-cost of the three to sustain at unpredictable capacity.

prompt: Which first-message opener is more likely to get a genuine reply?

options.text: 'Hi, excited to be here!'
'Hi, I'm stuck on debugging an async race condition, has anyone dealt with this?'

hints: A specific, concrete detail gives a reader something to actually respond to.
explanation: The specific opener names something concrete a reader can respond to directly. The generic one, while friendly, gives no actual opening for a reply.

prompt: Sort each.

items.text: You can do anything you set your mind to
Write your 'where I left off' note before closing the laptop, every time
Trust the process
Compare this month to three months ago, not to someone else's launch post

hints: Ask: could you literally act on this tomorrow, or does it just sound encouraging?
explanation: The concrete pieces name a specific action tied to a specific situation. The platitudes are true in a general sense but don't change what anyone actually does next.

prompt: Statement: all comparison to other people's work is corrosive and should be avoided entirely.

config.statement: All comparison to other people's work is corrosive and should be avoided entirely.
config.rubric: Should note that noticing a specific technique in someone else's finished work is a fair, useful comparison — the problem is specifically comparing your visible middle to their curated end, not comparison in general.

hints: Was every kind of comparison in this lesson labeled corrosive, or just a specific kind?
explanation: The lesson doesn't argue against all comparison — noticing and learning from a specific technique in someone else's work is genuinely useful. The corrosive pattern specifically is comparing your visible, unfinished middle to someone else's finished, edited end.
